newsitem.title: JAPAN: Minor Metals - Zaire casts shadow over cobalt market.
newsitem.headline: Minor Metals - Zaire casts shadow over cobalt market.

text.p: Cobalt prices remained strong on Tuesday, as a major deal between Zaire rebels and a U.S.- based company cast a shadow over Gecamines, the world's largest producer of the metal, Asian traders said.

"The deal has shown (Zaire's) rebels are ignoring what the Mobutu government has done in the past. There will be new problems leading to disturbances in its cobalt production," one trader at a major trading house in Japan said.

Last Wednesday, America Mineral Fields Inc (AMF) said it signed an agreement worth $1 billion with Zaire's rebels to buy the Kolwezi copper/cobalt tailings project and to build a 200,000 tonne a year zinc plant at Kipushi.
This surprised not only the Mobutu government, which denounced the deal immediately, but other companies that had been discussing mining projects with the Kinshasa government.

On Monday, South Africa's Anglo American Corp and De Beers Consolidated Mines Ltd said in Johannesburg that their senior executives were on their third visit to Zaire in less than a month to talk with rebels there.

Traders said while Gecamines production facilities seem now to be in the hands of rebels, questions remain on how they can reactivate the mines efficiently and whether they can rein in wildcat strikes that have hindered Gecamines production.

Earlier this week, a senior African industry source said most of Zaire's mines were now controlled by the rebels, but the facilities were undamaged and the next shipment of Zaire cobalt was likely to take place sometime this week.
Traders will be watching the Cobalt Development Institute meeting for users and producers which starts in Hong Kong on Wednesday.
A halt in U.S. stockpile cobalt shipments and sales until at least April 28 has also pushed up the price of the metal.
Some traders said the suspension led U.S. users to turn to the market to plug a gap of up to 1,000 tonnes.
In the magnesium market, prices were firm as China continued cutting its output, as the metal's price failed to cover production costs, Tokyo traders said.
Some traders expect the metal's price to recover towards $3,000 a tonne over the next one to two years, helped by Japan's strong demand for beverage cans.
On Monday, the Japan Aluminum Federation said Japan's 1996/97 output of aluminium sheet for beverage cans climbed 4.0 percent from the year before to a record 16,086 tonnes.
In Hong Kong, traders said the antimony market was quiet, with Chinese offers at $2,450 per tonne.
Bismuth fared better, with demand picking up and offers from overseas at $2.95/3.10 per pound feasible, and several containers were said to have been traded recently.

One 100-kg lot of germanium dioxide was said to have been sold to Japan last week at $780 per kg and another at $750 per kg, both CIF Japan. One 100-kg lot of germanium was also said to have been sold to Japan at $1,150 per kg.
One parcel of indium was said to have been sold last week to Japan at $285 per kg, CIF Japan.
